title: Building SoulWave: What I learned pushing generative AI to build a multiplayer arena game with a built-in VTuber studio and Spine animation tools
author: Just_Amoeba7123
selftext:
Hey everyone,

I wanted to share some thoughts and experiences from developing my indie game, SoulWave, a fast-paced 4-player multiplayer arena brawler built using a full-stack Node.js/Express, React, and HTML5 Canvas architecture.

When I started exploring generative AI coding assistants (Antigrafity, Cursor, and specifically working inside Google AI Studio with Gemini models), I didn't want to just make another generic text-based prototype. I wanted to see how far an agentic coding workflow could go when tasked with building a feature-rich, cohesive game complete with complex mechanics, custom physics, netcode via WebSockets, and heavy creative tools.

On the other hand, the friction points were very real. Generative AI frequently stumbled when trying to bridge the gap between DOM/React UI state and high-frequency Canvas rendering. For instance, syncing the custom Spine 2D animation timelines and the VTuber overlay composite rendering directly onto the game canvas resulted in a few early memory leaks and render-order desyncs. The AI would often suggest naive solutions that caused frame drops, requiring me to step in, profile the loops, and refactor the rendering pipeline manually.

Ultimately, using AI didn't mean "hands-off" development; it felt much more like working with an extremely fast, tireless junior developer who needs strict architectural boundaries and code reviews.

For those of you building games with AI assistance: how do you handle the architecture boundaries between your UI framework and your game loop? Have you found certain genres or systems where AI shines, and others where it completely falls apart?

**I started building a character editor. Somehow, it turned into a full multiplayer game.**

Hey everyone,

I wanted to share the story behind a project I've been working on for several months: **SoulWave**, a fast-paced multiplayer arena game that I'm building with HTML5 Canvas and a web-based architecture.

The funny thing is that SoulWave wasn't supposed to be a game at first.

It actually started as a **character editor** for another game I was working on. I wanted to build a modular system where I could experiment with characters, abilities, classes, animations, weapons, and other gameplay elements without having to rebuild everything from scratch.

Then I kept adding things.

The editor became more complex. Systems started interacting with each other. I began experimenting with combat, classes, maps, elemental mechanics, multiplayer, UI, shops, character customization, and all sorts of other systems.

At some point I realized I wasn't really building an editor anymore.

I was building a game.

I've been working on different parts of this project for months, usually adding or changing something whenever I had an idea. Now I'm at the point where I want to stop endlessly expanding the project and actually turn it into a complete, playable HTML game that I can release.

Currently, SoulWave already has a functional multiplayer system that I want to release with the game, along with systems for characters, classes, shops, and progression. There are currently **25 different classes** in the game, and I'm still experimenting with how everything fits together.

Generative AI has been a huge part of this process.

I've used several different AI tools during development, including Cursor, Antigravity, and Google AI Studio. So far, **Google AI Studio has worked the best for me**, especially because it can work with the project as a whole and help me iterate on large parts of the codebase.

But this is also where things get difficult.

The bigger the project becomes, the harder it is to make even a seemingly simple change.

Something that sounds like:

>

can suddenly affect the character system, combat logic, UI, animations, multiplayer state, balancing, or several other systems that I didn't even expect to be connected.

This has probably been the biggest lesson I've learned from using AI for game development:

**The AI can help me build things incredibly fast, but making changes safely becomes increasingly difficult as the project grows.**

I've had plenty of situations where an AI-generated change technically worked, but broke something somewhere else. Sometimes I have to spend much longer understanding what happened and fixing the architecture than I would have spent writing the original code myself. (I want to learn to do it one day...)

So I don't really see AI as "AI made my game."

It's closer to having an extremely fast development partner that can generate enormous amounts of code and ideas, but that also needs constant supervision, testing, architectural decisions, and debugging.

And that's actually what I'm most curious about with this project.

I'm now trying to figure out how far this workflow can realistically go: **Can a game that started as an AI-assisted collection of modular systems actually become a polished, complete multiplayer game that I can release?**
